title: The Ballad of Biggie and Tupac
summary: Josh and Chuck (with Jerry's production) tell the story of the rivalry between rappers Tupac Shakur and Biggie Smalls (Christopher Wallace), covering their early lives, their brief friendship, the Quad Recording Studios shooting, the East Coast vs. West Coast beef, the Source Awards speech by Suge Knight, the Soul Train Awards confrontation, Tupac's 1996 murder in Las Vegas, and Biggie's 1997 murder in Los Angeles. The episode closes with a listener email suggesting future topics and a note about what ended the East Coast-West Coast rivalry.
topics: East Coast vs West Coast rap beef

segments.title: Tour dates promo
segments.summary: Hosts promote upcoming tour stops in Denver, Seattle, and San Francisco and point listeners to the website for tickets.

segments.title: Opening and content warning
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the hip hop episode on Biggie and Tupac, warn that it contains adult content including violence and sexual assault, and frame the rivalry as the central East Coast vs. West Coast story of 1990s rap.

segments.title: Lifestyle pressure in hip hop
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how fans, media and the genre pushed rappers to act out the gangster lifestyle they rapped about, and how that contributed to the violence around them.

segments.title: Tupac's early life
segments.summary: Tupac was born in Harlem in 1971 to Afeni Shakur, a Panther 21 member acquitted in court. He was named after the Peruvian revolutionary Tupac Amaru II. His family moved to the Marin County area near San Francisco, and his mother struggled with crack addiction.

segments.title: Tupac's schooling and Digital Underground
segments.summary: Tupac was a strong English student who dropped out of high school and was mentored by teacher Leila Steinberg, who became his first manager. He was a dancer and performer with Digital Underground, whose Humpty Hump (Shock G) had a much less edgy style.

segments.title: Tupac's solo debut and early films
segments.summary: Tupac released a solo album, 2Pacalypse Now, which was underground rather than radio-friendly. Dan Quayle criticized the record. He began acting in Juice and Poetic Justice, and the hosts mention Above the Rim.

segments.title: Tupac's early run-ins with the law
segments.summary: Tupac became known for a thug reputation early on, including a shootout near the Marin County festival that killed a six-year-old and a 1993 incident in Atlanta involving off-duty police that was dismissed.

segments.title: Biggie's early life
segments.summary: Christopher Wallace (Biggie Smalls) was born in Brooklyn in 1972 to Jamaican immigrant parents. His mother, a preschool teacher, paid for a good high school, and he attended George Westinghouse, which had hip hop alumni. He later sold crack, dropped out, and got into trouble with police.

segments.title: Biggie's jail time and rise
segments.summary: Biggie spent nine months in jail. After his release he made a demo under the name Biggie Smalls, was listed in Source magazine's Unsigned Hype column in 1992, and was noticed by Sean Combs, who signed him to Bad Boy.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode sponsor break.

segments.title: Tupac and Biggie's friendship and the seed of beef
segments.summary: Tupac and Biggie met in 1993 and became close; Tupac mentored Biggie and Biggie stayed on his couch in LA. Biggie asked Tupac to manage him, but Tupac advised him to stay with Combs. Combs grew jealous of their friendship, and Tupac considered him a poser. Ready to Die (1994) was a double platinum hit that brought the rap spotlight back to New York.

segments.title: Haitian Jack and the Ayana Jackson case
segments.summary: In 1993, while Tupac was filming in New York, Haitian Jack began hanging around him, and Biggie warned him against Jack. Ayana Jackson alleged Tupac, Haitian Jack, Charles Fuller and another man assaulted her; police found guns. Tupac later told the New York Daily News that Haitian Jack cooperated with police, and the two split.

segments.title: Quad Recording Studios shooting
segments.summary: Tupac, financially strapped, agreed to a guest spot for rapper Little Sean for $7,000 at Quad Recording Studios in Times Square on November 30, 1994. Three men robbed, shot and beat him. Combs and Biggie were upstairs, and Tupac flipped them off from his gurney, believing they were involved, which started the beef.

segments.title: Tupac's trial and imprisonment
segments.summary: Tupac was convicted of sexual abuse and acquitted of other charges, sentenced to eighteen months in prison, and his album Me Against the World was released while he was incarcerated.

segments.title: Who Shot Ya and Tupac's paranoia
segments.summary: While Tupac was in prison, Biggie released Who Shot Ya, which Tupac took as aimed at him. The hosts say evidence suggests Biggie wrote it before the Quad shooting and that Tupac's suspicions were likely fueled by mental health issues.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Sponsor break.

segments.title: Rival labels Bad Boy and Death Row
segments.summary: Death Row Records was founded in 1992 by Dr. Dre and others, with Suge Knight as CEO; Bad Boy was run by Sean Combs. The hosts contrast the two labels and Knight's gang ties.

segments.title: Source Awards speech and hosts' music opinions
segments.summary: At the 1995 Source Awards, Suge Knight publicly invited rappers to Death Row, a jab at Combs's habit of appearing in videos. The hosts discuss Combs's image and share personal favorite rap albums and artists.

segments.title: Club Platinum shooting and Tupac's release
segments.summary: In September 1995 at the Platinum House strip club in Atlanta, a fight broke out between Death Row and Bad Boy associates; Death Row employee Jake Robles was shot and killed. Tupac was released on bail, and his album All Eyes on Me reached number one.

segments.title: Faith Evans and Tupac's feud
segments.summary: After his release, Tupac hired Faith Evans, Biggie's wife, for $25,000 to sing on All Eyes on Me. She went to a hotel room afterward and says she was propositioned; she denies sex occurred. Tupac publicly claimed they had sex.

segments.title: Soul Train Awards confrontation and Hit Em Up
segments.summary: At the March 1996 Soul Train Awards, Tupac and Biggie both won awards with their crews; a standoff with guns drawn followed but no one was shot. Tupac released Hit 'Em Up, a diss track naming Biggie.

segments.title: Tupac's murder in Las Vegas
segments.summary: After the September 7, 1996 Mike Tyson fight in Las Vegas, Orlando Anderson was beaten by Death Row associates after an alleged necklace theft. Hours later, a Cadillac pulled up at a stoplight and shot Tupac and Suge Knight; Tupac died six days later at age 25.

segments.title: Keith D and the Tupac murder case
segments.summary: Keith D admitted in a 2019 memoir that he was in the Cadillac. Anderson was later killed in Compton. Keith D was arrested in September 2023 and charged with Tupac's murder, with trial scheduled for August 2026. The hosts also mention the Tupac statue in Clarkston, Georgia.

segments.title: Biggie's murder in Los Angeles and aftermath
segments.summary: Biggie was shot in March 1997 in a car after a Vibe party in LA and died at age 24. Suge Knight was suspected, though he was not charged. Biggie's album Life After Death was released and sold over ten million copies. Suge Knight is serving a 28-year sentence and hosts a jail podcast.

segments.title: End of the rivalry and Michael Jackson rumor
segments.summary: Hosts credit Outkast with ending the East Coast-West Coast rivalry by diminishing regional divisions. They relay a widespread rumor that Michael Jackson assaulted Tupac after he insulted Quincy Jones's daughter, and that Biggie appeared on a Jackson song.

segments.title: Listener mail from Josiah
segments.summary: A listener from Tennessee praises the show and suggests future topics including Anne Frank, Oskar Schindler, Motown, Mister Rogers and the Hindenburg, which is already in the works.
